title: Wrapper Classes
description: The object wrappers for each primitive type, autoboxing/unboxing, and the pitfalls they introduce.
objectives: Know each primitive type's wrapper class

content.heading: Wrapper Classes and Autoboxing
content.body:
Every primitive type has a corresponding wrapper class: int/Integer, double/Double, char/Character, boolean/Boolean, and similarly for the others. Wrapper classes exist because primitives cannot be used where an object is required — generic type parameters (List<int> is illegal; List<Integer> is required), and anywhere the code specifically needs null as a possible value (a primitive can never be null).

Autoboxing is the compiler's automatic conversion from a primitive to its wrapper (Integer x = 5; — really Integer.valueOf(5) behind the scenes); unboxing is the reverse (int y = someInteger; calls someInteger.intValue()). This happens transparently almost everywhere a primitive/wrapper mismatch would otherwise require an explicit conversion, including inside collections: adding an int to a List<Integer> autoboxes it automatically.

content.heading: Wrapper Pitfalls
content.body:
Wrapper classes are objects, so == on two wrapper references compares identity, not value — exactly like String. Java caches (interns) small Integer values from -128 to 127 for performance, so Integer a = 100, b = 100; a == b happens to be true, but Integer a = 200, b = 200; a == b is false, since 200 falls outside the cached range — a notoriously confusing inconsistency that reinforces why .equals() (or, better, comparing the unboxed primitives directly) should always be used to compare wrapper values, never ==.

Unboxing a null wrapper throws a NullPointerException: if an Integer variable is null and you use it in an int context (like arithmetic, or assigning to an int), Java attempts to unbox it automatically and crashes — this is a common, easy-to-miss source of NPEs, especially with values coming from a Map.get() that might return null.

content.explanation: The a == b vs c == d inconsistency happens purely because of Integer's internal caching of small values — it's a trap, not something to rely on. .equals() always gives the correct, consistent answer for wrapper value comparison.

keyPoints: Every primitive has a wrapper class (int/Integer, double/Double, etc.), needed for generics and nullability
Autoboxing/unboxing convert between primitives and wrappers automatically
Never use == to compare wrapper values — small-integer caching makes it inconsistent; use .equals()
Unboxing a null wrapper throws NullPointerException
commonMistakes: Comparing wrapper objects with == and getting inconsistent results depending on the value's magnitude
Unboxing a possibly-null wrapper (e.g., from Map.get()) without a null check first
Using List<int> instead of List<Integer>, not realizing generics require a reference type
